claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain rates in fusion plasma-facing structural materials are primarily governed by vacancy-mediated dislocation-climb kinetics.
Toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is primarily governed by vacancy-mediated dislocation-climb kinetics.
Microalloying additions can systematically alter vacancy diffusion.
Selected microalloying additions can modify the activation energy for vacancy migration without significantly altering the overall microstructure.
Added solutes adjust the energy barrier for vacancy migration.
Changing the vacancy-migration energy barrier accelerates or retards vacancy-mediated dislocation climb.
Changes in vacancy kinetics and dislocation climb alter the rate of high-temperature plastic deformation.
Changes in vacancy kinetics and dislocation climb alter material toughness.
A microalloyed variant with higher vacancy-migration activation energy and reduced vacancy mobility will have a lower high-temperature plastic strain rate than the unperturbed baseline.
A microalloyed variant with reduced vacancy mobility will have higher toughness than the unperturbed baseline.
Microalloying that increases vacancy mobility will produce a higher high-temperature strain rate.
Microalloying that increases vacancy mobility will reduce toughness.
The proposed relationships apply in high-temperature regimes where vacancy diffusion and dislocation climb are prominent.
The proposed relationships require the microstructural state to remain comparable between samples aside from solute content.
Prior experimental trends support a role for vacancy-mediated climb.
The quantitative effects of specific solute additions and their interactions with irradiation are uncertain.
